Title: Latest headlines about the pandemic
Commentary:
In England, infections, hospitalisations and deaths started increasing in December 2020. The infection rate and hospital admission rate have decreased in recent weeks. Cases compatible with the new UK variant of COVID-19 decreased in England, Wales and Northern Ireland.

The number of deaths involving the coronavirus (COVID-19) decreased in the latest week in England and Wales, but total deaths remain above the five-year average. Despite recent increases, most people do not have antibodies to COVID-19. This suggests most of the population remains vulnerable to infection.

Title: Coronavirus (COVID-19) pandemic
Commentary:
The percentage of people testing positive for the coronavirus (COVID-19) has decreased in all four UK countries in recent weeks. In the week ending 6 February 2021, it is estimated that 1 in 80 people in England, 1 in 85 in Wales, 1 in 75 in Northern Ireland, and 1 in 150 in Scotland were infected.

In the week ending 7 February, hospital admission rates decreased to 19 per 100,000 people. The number of registered deaths involving COVID-19 in England and Wales decreased in the week ending 5 February. Over 42% of all deaths recorded that week involved COVID-19. It is estimated that around 1 in 5 people in England had antibodies against COVID-19 in the 28 days to 1 February.

Title: Coronavirus (COVID-19) infections
Commentary: The percentage of people testing positive for the coronavirus (COVID-19) has decreased in England, Wales, Northern Ireland and Scotland (week ending 6 February 2021). In England around 1 in 80 people in the community population had COVID-19. Around 1 in 85 in Wales, 1 in 75 in Northern Ireland and 1 in 150 people in Scotland were infected. London continues to have the highest infection rate of all regions in England. Cases compatible with the new UK variant decreased in England, Wales and Northern Ireland.

Title: Hospital admissions with coronavirus (COVID-19)
Commentary:
Hospital admissions of COVID-19-confirmed patients in England started increasing in early December 2020, but have decreased in recent weeks. Rates fell in the week ending 7 February 2021, but remain high at 19 per 100,000 people. This is almost half the rate seen in the week ending 17 January 2021. In the most recent week, hospital admission rates decreased in all regions in England. The highest rates were seen in the West Midlands.

Data on hospital admissions presented here are collected by Public Health England and available on the government dashboard and national flu and COVID-19 surveillance reports.

Data on coronavirus confirmed hospital admissions for other nations are available on Northern Ireland Department of Health webpage, Scottish Government webpage and Public Health Wales dashboard.

Title: Deaths involving coronavirus (COVID-19)
Commentary:
The number of deaths registered in England and Wales in the week ending 5 February 2021 was 17,192. Just under half (7,320) of these deaths mentioned coronavirus on the death certificate, a decrease from the previous week. However, the total number of deaths registered was 40.8% higher than the five-year average.

Weekly death registrations for Scotland and Northern Ireland are produced and published by National Records of Scotland and Northern Ireland Statistics and Research Agency..

Title: Impact of coronavirus (COVID-19) on society
Commentary:
The percentage of people compliant with preventative measures to curb the spread of COVID-19, such as hand washing and the use of face coverings, remained high in Great Britain in the week ending 7 February 2021. The proportion of adults reporting staying at home or only leaving for work, exercise, essential shopping or medical needs in the past seven days remains higher than during the winter 2020 restrictions (prior to the early-2021 lockdown).

Most personal well-being scores remained at some of the lowest levels since March 2020, although the anxiety score has improved since early January 2021. Just over 1 in 4 (27%) adults felt that it will take more than a year for life to return to normal. Around 3 in 4 adults (74%) would take part in mass testing if it was available in their area.

Title: Impact of coronavirus (COVID-19) pandemic on different age groups
Commentary: Coronavirus (COVID-19) infection rates decreased in all age groups (week ending 6 February 2021). Adults aged 34 to 49 years had the highest percentage of people testing positive, while those aged 70 years and over had the lowest. Hospital admission rates have decreased or remained level in all age groups (week ending 7 February). Even though more young people are infected, hospital admissions and deaths involving COVID-19 are highest in those aged 65 years and over. Nearly three-quarters of deaths involving COVID-19 have been in people aged 75 years and over.

Title: Overview of coronavirus  (COVID-19) pandemic by UK geographic area
Commentary: The percentage of people testing positive for the coronavirus (COVID-19) decreased in all regions in England (week ending 6 February 2021), except in the South West where the rate appears level. Despite recent decreases, London continues to have the highest positivity rate. COVID-19 confirmed hospital admission rates fell in all regions in England, with the largest decrease in the West Midlands (week ending 7 February). The number of deaths involving COVID-19 decreased in all regions in England in the week ending 5 February for the first time since July, although the total number of deaths registered was higher than the five-year average in all English regions and Wales for the 13th week in a row.

Title: Impact of coronavirus (COVID-19) pandemic on different ethnic groups
Commentary:
People from ethnic minorities are more likely to test positive for COVID-19 compared with white ethnic groups. COVID-19 death rates are also higher for most ethnic minorities compared with white ethnic groups. This is in part because of the types of jobs and housing more common among ethnic minorities, but this does not completely explain the disparity.

People from minority ethnic groups are less likely to say they would have the COVID-19 vaccine. Further ethnicity statistics are available on the Ethnicity Facts and Figures website.

Title: Coronavirus (COVID-19) pandemic in schools
Commentary: A study conducted in November 2020 found no meaningful difference in positivity rates between primary and secondary schools. These findings cannot be applied to England as a whole as only a sample of local authorities were studied. However, this initial information will inform further research. This research was conducted in partnership with the ONS, the School of Hygiene and Tropical Medicine, and Public Health England.

Title: Impact of coronavirus (COVID-19) pandemic on higher education
Commentary:
The ONS has been working with higher education bodies to understand the impact of the pandemic on students. In 2020, most students said their mental health had worsened as a result of the coronavirus.

Initial research into the spread of COVID-19 among students, using case studies from the universities of Exeter and Loughborough, found a peak in cases following the start of the autumn term in 2020. Although these statistics are experimental, and findings are not applicable nationwide, they provide important information that will inform further research.

Title: Antibodies against coronavirus (COVID-19)
Commentary: Antibodies against COVID-19 suggest that a person previously had the infection or has been vaccinated against the coronavirus. The percentage of people testing positive for antibodies increased to around 1 in 5 people in England, 1 in 7 people in Wales, 1 in 9 people in Scotland and 1 in 7 people in Northern Ireland in the 28 days to 1 February. People aged 80 years and over were most likely to test positive for antibodies in England, those aged 16 to 24 years in Wales and Scotland, and those aged 25 to 34 years in Northern Ireland. London had the highest antibody positivity among English regions.

Title: Coronavirus (COVID-19) vaccination
Commentary:
Over 9 in 10 (92%) people said they had either received the COVID-19 vaccine, had accepted an offer and were awaiting vaccination, or would be likely to have the vaccine if offered (week ending 7 February 2021) Around 1 in 5 (22%) of adults reported receiving at least one dose of the vaccine, compared with 16% last week. Older adults are more likely to say they would accept or have already received the vaccine than younger adults. Fewer people in minority ethnic groups said they would be likely to have the vaccine than in White ethnic groups (10 December 2020 to 10 January 2021).

Official data on the number of people who have received a COVID-19 vaccination is collated by Public Health England and is available on the government dashboard.
